stem: State what is meant by electric current, and name the unit it is measured in.

marking.point: Current is the rate of flow of electrical charge
Measured in amperes / amps (A)

answer_text: Electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge. It is measured in amperes (A).

stem: A current of 0.25 A flows through a lamp for 240 seconds. Calculate the charge that flows.

marking.point: Q = I t

stem: Which component is used to measure the current in a circuit, and how is it connected?

marking.point: An ammeter, connected in series

stem: Explain why a circuit must be complete for a current to flow.

marking.point: Charge must have a continuous conducting path to flow around
If there is a break / gap, the charge cannot flow and the current is zero

answer_text: Charge needs a continuous conducting loop to move around. If the circuit is broken anywhere, there is no complete path, so no charge flows and the current is zero.

stem: A resistor has a potential difference of 6.0 V across it and a current of 0.40 A through it. Calculate its resistance.
equation: V = I R,  so R = V / I

marking.point: R = V / I

stem: State what is meant by the potential difference across a component, and name its unit.

marking.point: The energy transferred per unit charge passing through the component
Measured in volts (V)

answer_text: Potential difference is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge passing through the component. It is measured in volts.

stem: Describe how you would investigate the effect of the length of a wire on its resistance.

marking.point: Connect the wire in series with an ammeter and a power supply, with a voltmeter across the wire
Use a crocodile clip on a metre rule to vary the length, measuring each length
Record current and potential difference for each length and calculate R = V / I
Keep the wire material, thickness and supply p.d. the same, and switch off between readings so the wire does not heat up

answer_text: Set up the wire in series with an ammeter and power supply, with a voltmeter across the wire. Lay the wire along a metre rule and use a crocodile clip to select a measured length. For each length record the current and potential difference and work out R = V / I. Keep the wire's material, thickness and the supply p.d. constant, and switch off between readings so the wire does not warm up and change its resistance. Plot resistance against length.

stem: Explain, in terms of the movement of charge, why the resistance of a metal wire increases as its temperature rises.

marking.point: The ions in the metal vibrate more as temperature increases
So there are more collisions between the electrons and the ions
This makes it harder for charge to flow, so the resistance increases

answer_text: As the temperature rises the metal ions vibrate with greater amplitude. The flowing electrons then collide with them more frequently, which opposes the flow of charge and so increases the resistance of the wire.

stem: Describe the shape of the current–potential difference graph for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, and state what it shows.

marking.point: A straight line through the origin
showing current is directly proportional to potential difference, so resistance is constant

answer_text: It is a straight line through the origin. This shows the current is directly proportional to the potential difference, so the resistance stays constant.

stem: Explain the shape of the current–potential difference graph for a filament lamp.

marking.point: The graph is a curve that becomes less steep as p.d. increases
As current increases the filament gets hotter
The higher temperature increases the resistance, so the current rises less rapidly

answer_text: The graph is an S-shaped curve that flattens as the potential difference rises. A larger current heats the filament, and the higher temperature increases its resistance, so each extra volt produces a smaller increase in current.

stem: What happens to the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) as the light gets brighter?

marking.point: It decreases

stem: A diode is connected into a circuit. Explain why there is a current in one direction but not the other.

marking.point: A diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction
so charge cannot flow / the current is almost zero that way round

answer_text: A diode has a very low resistance in the forward direction but a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so charge can flow one way but essentially no current flows the other way.

stem: Three resistors of 12 Ω, 18 Ω and 20 Ω are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit.

marking.point: Resistances in series add

stem: Two identical lamps are connected in series to a 6 V battery. State the potential difference across each lamp and explain your answer.

marking.point: 3 V across each lamp
because the total p.d. of the supply is shared between components in series, and the lamps are identical

answer_text: Each lamp has 3 V across it. In a series circuit the supply potential difference is shared between the components, and because the lamps are identical they have equal resistance so they share it equally.

stem: Explain why adding a second resistor in parallel to a circuit decreases the total resistance.

marking.point: Adding a parallel branch gives the charge an additional path to flow through
The total current from the supply increases for the same potential difference
Since R = V / I, a larger current at the same p.d. means a smaller total resistance

answer_text: A second parallel resistor creates an extra route for charge to flow, so more current is drawn from the supply for the same potential difference. Since R = V / I, a bigger current at unchanged p.d. means the total resistance has fallen — it is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

stem: Explain one advantage of wiring the lamps in a house in parallel rather than in series.

marking.point: Each lamp gets the full supply potential difference / can be switched independently
If one lamp breaks the others still work, because the other branches remain complete

answer_text: In parallel each lamp receives the full mains potential difference and can be switched on and off independently. If one lamp fails, the other branches are still complete circuits, so the remaining lamps keep working.

stem: State the frequency and the potential difference of the UK domestic mains electricity supply.

marking.point: Frequency 50 Hz
About 230 V

answer_text: UK mains electricity is an alternating supply with a frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V.

stem: Explain the difference between direct potential difference and alternating potential difference.

marking.point: Direct p.d. is always in the same direction, so the current is in one direction only
Alternating p.d. repeatedly changes direction, so the current continually reverses

answer_text: A direct potential difference always acts in the same direction, producing a current that flows one way only. An alternating potential difference repeatedly changes direction, so the current continually reverses.

stem: Explain the purpose of the earth wire in a mains appliance with a metal case.

marking.point: The earth wire is a safety wire connected to the metal case
If a live wire touches the case, a large current flows to earth through the earth wire
This large current melts the fuse or trips the circuit breaker, disconnecting the supply and preventing electric shock

answer_text: The earth wire is a safety wire joining the metal case to earth. If a fault lets the live wire touch the case, a very large current flows through the earth wire to earth. That surge melts the fuse or trips the circuit breaker, cutting off the supply so the case cannot give anyone a shock.

stem: Explain why touching the live wire of a mains supply can give an electric shock, even if you are not touching the neutral wire.

marking.point: The live wire is at about 230 V while your body is at earth potential (0 V)
so there is a large potential difference across you and a current flows through you to earth

answer_text: The live wire sits at around 230 V while your body is at earth potential, 0 V. That large potential difference drives a current through your body to earth, which is what causes the shock.

stem: A heater works at 230 V and draws a current of 8.0 A. Calculate its power.

marking.point: P = V I

stem: A current of 3.0 A flows through a 25 Ω resistor. Calculate the power dissipated.

marking.point: P = I² R

stem: A charge of 1500 C flows through a motor. The potential difference across the motor is 12 V. Calculate the energy transferred.

marking.point: E = Q V

stem: Explain why the plug and cable of a high-power appliance such as an electric shower get warm during use.

marking.point: There is a large current in the cable, and the cable has some resistance
Work is done against this resistance, transferring energy to the thermal store of the cable

answer_text: A high-power appliance draws a large current, and the cable has some resistance. Work done against that resistance transfers energy to the thermal store of the cable and plug, so they warm up.

stem: State the purpose of a step-up transformer and a step-down transformer in the National Grid.

marking.point: Step-up transformers increase the potential difference for transmission
Step-down transformers reduce it to a safe level for consumers

answer_text: Step-up transformers raise the potential difference before electricity is transmitted across the grid. Step-down transformers lower it again to a safe value for homes and businesses.

stem: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference.

marking.point: For a given power, P = V I, so a higher potential difference means a smaller current
Energy is dissipated in the cables at a rate given by P = I² R
Because the power loss depends on the current squared, a small reduction in current gives a large reduction in loss
so the transmission is more efficient / less energy is wasted as heating

answer_text: The power delivered is P = V I, so transmitting at a very high potential difference means the current can be small. The power wasted heating the cables is P = I² R, which depends on the square of the current, so cutting the current sharply reduces the losses. Transmission is therefore far more efficient.

stem: Why can transformers not be used in a system that transmits electricity using direct current?
choices: Transformers need a changing magnetic field, which d.c. does not produce
Direct current has too high a frequency
Transformers would melt if used with d.c.

marking.point: Transformers need a changing magnetic field, which a steady direct current does not produce

stem: Explain why the National Grid is described as an efficient way of transferring energy across a country.

marking.point: Transmitting at high p.d. and low current keeps energy losses in the cables small
so most of the energy generated reaches consumers

answer_text: By transmitting at very high potential difference and correspondingly low current, the energy wasted heating the transmission cables is kept small, so most of the energy generated at the power station actually reaches consumers.

stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry cloth and becomes negatively charged. Explain how the rod becomes charged.

marking.point: Friction causes electrons to be transferred between the cloth and the rod
Electrons move from the cloth onto the rod
The rod gains electrons so becomes negatively charged, and the cloth is left positively charged

answer_text: Rubbing transfers electrons by friction. Electrons move from the cloth onto the polythene rod, so the rod gains negative charge while the cloth, having lost electrons, is left equally positively charged.

stem: Two objects both carry a positive charge. What force acts between them?

marking.point: Repulsion

stem: Describe the electric field around an isolated negatively charged sphere.

marking.point: The field lines are radial / straight lines along the radius
They point inwards, towards the centre of the sphere
The field is strongest closest to the sphere, where the lines are closest together

answer_text: The field lines are radial, pointing inwards towards the centre of the sphere because the field direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge. The lines are closest together near the surface, showing the field is strongest there and gets weaker with distance.

stem: As a charged object is brought closer to an earthed metal plate, a spark eventually jumps across the gap. Explain why.

marking.point: As the separation decreases, the electric field strength between them increases
A strong enough field ionises the air in the gap, so the air conducts
Electrons then flow across the gap, and the energy transferred produces the spark

answer_text: Bringing the object closer increases the electric field strength in the gap. Once the field is strong enough it ionises the air particles, stripping electrons from them so the air becomes a conductor. Charge then flows across the gap, and the energy released is seen and heard as a spark.

stem: A cyclist freewheels down a hill and speeds up. Which energy store increases?

marking.point: Kinetic

stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards and rises to its highest point. Describe the energy transfers that take place as the ball rises.

marking.point: Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of the ball
to the gravitational potential store of the ball
Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings by air resistance

answer_text: As the ball rises, energy is transferred from its kinetic store to its gravitational potential store. A small amount is also transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings because of air resistance.

stem: State what is meant by a closed system, and state what happens to the total energy of a closed system.

marking.point: A closed system is one where no energy (or matter) enters or leaves
The net change in the total energy of a closed system is always zero

answer_text: A closed system is one in which no energy transfers into or out of the system. The net change in its total energy is always zero — energy is only redistributed between stores.

stem: A kettle is switched on and the water inside boils. Describe the main energy transfer.

marking.point: Energy is transferred electrically (by the heating element / by work done by the current)
to the thermal store of the water

answer_text: Energy is transferred electrically from the mains to the heating element, and from there to the thermal energy store of the water.

stem: A runner of mass 62 kg is moving at 8.0 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy of the runner.

marking.point: 1984 J (allow 2000 J to 2 s.f.)

stem: A crane lifts a 450 kg load through a vertical height of 12 m. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy of the load.

marking.point: Ep = m g h

stem: A spring of spring constant 250 N/m is compressed by 0.080 m. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.

marking.point: Ee = 0.5 k e²

stem: A ball is dropped from rest and falls towards the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Explain how you could use energy transfer to find the speed of the ball just before it lands, if you know the height it fell from.

marking.point: The gravitational potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained
m g h = 0.5 m v²
The mass cancels, giving v² = 2 g h
so v = √(2 g h) — the speed does not depend on the mass

answer_text: With no air resistance the system is closed, so all the gravitational potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy: m g h = ½ m v². The mass cancels from both sides, leaving v² = 2gh, so v = √(2gh). Notably the landing speed does not depend on the mass of the ball.

stem: State what is meant by the specific heat capacity of a substance.

marking.point: The energy needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance
by one degree Celsius

answer_text: The specific heat capacity is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.

stem: A 0.35 kg block of aluminium is heated from 18 °C to 58 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the block.
In an experiment, 18 000 J of energy is transferred to a 1.5 kg metal block. The temperature of the block rises by 30 °C. Determine the specific heat capacity of the metal.
equation: ΔE = m c Δθ,  so c = ΔE / (m Δθ)

marking.point: Rearranges to c = ΔE / (m Δθ)
400 J/kg °C

stem: In an experiment to find the specific heat capacity of a metal block, the value obtained is higher than the accepted value. Explain why.

marking.point: Energy is transferred to the surroundings / lost as thermal energy
So the measured energy input is greater than the energy that actually heated the block
Since c = ΔE / (m Δθ), too large an ΔE gives too large a value of c

answer_text: Some of the energy supplied is transferred to the surroundings rather than to the block, so the energy recorded is larger than the energy that actually raised the block's temperature. Because c = ΔE / (m Δθ), an ΔE that is too large gives a specific heat capacity that is too high. Insulating the block reduces this.

stem: Which of these is the correct definition of power?
choices: The energy transferred per unit time
The force applied per unit area
The work done per unit distance

marking.point: The energy transferred per unit time

stem: A motor transfers 45 000 J of energy in 90 seconds. Calculate the power of the motor.

marking.point: P = E / t

stem: A hoist does 24 000 J of work lifting a load in 40 s. A second hoist does the same work in 30 s. Calculate how much greater the power of the second hoist is, in watts.

marking.point: Difference = 200 W

stem: Two lamps transfer the same amount of energy. Lamp A has a higher power rating than lamp B. Explain what this tells you about the time each lamp was switched on.

marking.point: Lamp A transfers the energy in a shorter time
because power is energy transferred per second, so for the same energy a higher power means less time

answer_text: Lamp A must have been on for a shorter time. Power is the energy transferred per second, so for the same total energy the higher-power lamp takes less time.

stem: Explain what is meant by dissipated energy.

marking.point: Energy that is transferred to the surroundings / to less useful stores
It is spread out and becomes less useful, though it is not destroyed

answer_text: Dissipated energy is energy transferred to stores that are not useful — usually the thermal store of the surroundings. It is not destroyed, but it becomes spread out and can no longer be used usefully.

stem: Explain how lubricating the moving parts of a machine reduces unwanted energy transfer.

marking.point: Lubrication reduces friction between the moving surfaces
Less work is done against friction, so less energy is transferred to thermal stores
so more of the input energy is transferred usefully / efficiency increases

answer_text: A lubricant reduces the friction between surfaces that rub together. Less work is then done against friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the machine and surroundings, and a greater fraction of the input energy is transferred usefully.

stem: Describe an investigation to compare how well different materials work as thermal insulators, using beakers of hot water.

marking.point: Wrap identical beakers in different insulating materials of the same thickness
Pour the same volume of water at the same starting temperature into each
Measure the temperature of each at regular intervals with a thermometer or datalogger
The best insulator is the one whose water cools by the least in the same time

answer_text: Wrap several identical beakers in different insulating materials of equal thickness, and leave one unwrapped as a control. Add the same volume of water at the same starting temperature to each, cover with a lid, and record the temperature of each every minute for a fixed time. The material whose water shows the smallest temperature drop is the best insulator.

stem: Explain why thicker walls reduce the rate of energy transfer out of a house.

marking.point: Energy has to be conducted through a greater thickness of material
which lowers the rate of energy transfer by conduction

answer_text: Thicker walls mean energy must be conducted through a greater thickness of material, which reduces the rate of energy transfer by conduction and so keeps the house warmer for longer.

stem: A motor is supplied with 8000 J of energy and transfers 5600 J usefully. Calculate the efficiency of the motor.
equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer

marking.point: efficiency = useful / total

stem: A lamp has a power input of 60 W and is 0.15 efficient. Calculate the useful power output of the lamp.
equation: efficiency = useful power output / total power input

marking.point: useful power output = efficiency × total power input

stem: Why can no practical device ever be 100% efficient?
choices: Energy is always destroyed in the device
Some energy is always dissipated to less useful stores
The input energy can never be measured accurately
Efficiency is defined as always less than one

marking.point: Some energy is always dissipated to less useful stores

stem: An electric kettle is about 90% efficient, but a filament lamp is only about 5% efficient. Explain why the kettle is so much more efficient.

marking.point: For a kettle the useful output is the thermal store of the water
Almost all the electrical energy is transferred to that thermal store, with only a little lost to the kettle body and surroundings
For a lamp the useful output is light, but most of the energy is transferred to thermal stores instead, which is wasted

answer_text: In a kettle the useful output is the thermal energy of the water, and nearly all the electrical input ends up there — only a little escapes to the kettle body and surroundings. In a filament lamp the useful output is light, but the filament transfers most of its energy to thermal stores, so only a small fraction of the input becomes light.

stem: Explain the difference between a renewable and a non-renewable energy resource.

marking.point: A renewable resource is replenished as it is used / will not run out
A non-renewable resource is finite and will eventually run out

answer_text: A renewable energy resource is one that is replenished as fast as it is used, so it will not run out. A non-renewable resource is finite — once used it cannot be replaced on a human timescale.

stem: Which of these is a non-renewable energy resource?

marking.point: Nuclear fuel

stem: A country is deciding whether to build a new wind farm or a new gas-fired power station. Give two advantages and two disadvantages of choosing the wind farm.

marking.point: Advantage: renewable, so will not run out
Advantage: no carbon dioxide emitted during use, so does not add to global warming
Disadvantage: unreliable — output depends on the wind
Disadvantage: high set-up cost, visual or noise pollution, or needs a large area of land

answer_text: Advantages: wind is renewable so will not run out, and no carbon dioxide is released while generating, so it does not contribute to global warming. Disadvantages: output is unreliable because it depends on the wind, and wind farms have high set-up costs and cause visual and noise pollution over a large area.

stem: Many countries have increased their use of renewable energy resources over the last twenty years, even though renewables are often more expensive to build. Explain why.

marking.point: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to global warming / climate change
Fossil fuels are finite and will eventually run out, and prices may rise
Governments have responded to environmental pressure or international agreements / targets

answer_text: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants, driving global warming and acid rain. Fossil fuels are also finite, so supplies will run out and become more expensive. Political and public pressure, along with international climate agreements, has pushed governments to switch despite the higher set-up costs.

stem: Explain the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity.

marking.point: A scalar has magnitude (size) only
A vector has both magnitude and direction

answer_text: A scalar quantity has only a magnitude, such as speed or mass. A vector quantity has both a magnitude and a direction, such as velocity or force.

stem: Which of these is a vector quantity?

marking.point: Acceleration

stem: A car drives once around a circular track and returns to its starting point. Explain why its average velocity is zero but its average speed is not.

marking.point: Velocity uses displacement, which is zero because the car ends where it started
Speed uses total distance travelled, which is the full length of the track and is not zero

answer_text: Average velocity uses displacement — the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish — which is zero because the car returns to its starting point. Average speed uses the total distance travelled, the whole circumference, which is definitely not zero.

stem: Describe how a vector quantity is represented on a diagram.

marking.point: By an arrow
The length of the arrow shows the magnitude and the direction it points shows the direction

answer_text: A vector is drawn as an arrow. The length of the arrow, drawn to scale, represents the magnitude, and the direction the arrow points represents the direction of the quantity.

stem: Explain the difference between a contact force and a non-contact force, giving one example of each.

marking.point: A contact force acts only when objects are physically touching, e.g. friction, air resistance, tension or normal contact force
A non-contact force acts when objects are physically separated, e.g. gravitational, magnetic or electrostatic force

answer_text: A contact force acts only when two objects are physically touching, such as friction or the normal contact force. A non-contact force acts even when the objects are separated, such as the gravitational, magnetic or electrostatic force.

stem: Explain the difference between the mass and the weight of an object.

marking.point: Mass is the amount of matter in the object, a scalar measured in kilograms, and it does not change with location
Weight is the force acting on the object due to gravity, a vector measured in newtons, which depends on the gravitational field strength

answer_text: Mass is the quantity of matter in an object. It is a scalar, measured in kilograms, and is the same everywhere. Weight is the force on the object due to a gravitational field. It is a vector, measured in newtons, and changes if the gravitational field strength changes.

stem: A bag of cement has a mass of 25 kg. Gravitational field strength on Earth is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate its weight.

marking.point: W = m g

stem: State what is meant by the centre of mass of an object, and state where the weight of an object is taken to act.

marking.point: The centre of mass is the single point at which the mass of the object may be considered to be concentrated
The weight is considered to act at the centre of mass

answer_text: The centre of mass is the single point where the whole mass of the object can be taken to be concentrated. The weight of the object is considered to act at that point.

stem: A box is pushed to the right with a force of 85 N. Friction of 32 N acts to the left. Calculate the resultant force on the box.

marking.point: Forces in opposite directions subtract
85 − 32 = 53 N to the right

stem: State what is meant by the resultant force on an object, and state what it means if the resultant force is zero.

marking.point: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on the object combined
If it is zero the forces are balanced, so the object stays at rest or continues at constant velocity

answer_text: The resultant force is the single force that would have the same effect as all the individual forces acting together. If it is zero the forces are balanced, so the object either stays at rest or keeps moving at a constant velocity.

stem: Two forces act on an object at right angles: 6.0 N to the east and 8.0 N to the north. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force.

marking.point: Recognises the resultant is the diagonal of a right-angled triangle
R = 10 N

stem: A book rests on a table. Describe the forces acting on the book and explain why it stays at rest.

marking.point: The weight of the book acts downwards
The normal contact force from the table acts upwards
The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero and the book remains at rest

answer_text: Two forces act: the weight of the book pulling down, and the normal contact force from the table pushing up. They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero and by Newton's First Law the book stays at rest.

stem: A force of 240 N pushes a crate 6.5 m along the floor in the direction of the force. Calculate the work done.

marking.point: W = F s

stem: State what is meant by work done, and state the relationship between the joule and the newton-metre.

marking.point: Work is done when a force causes an object to move through a distance (energy is transferred)
One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre, so 1 J = 1 N m

answer_text: Work is done whenever a force causes an object to move through a distance, and the work done equals the energy transferred. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object through one metre, so 1 J = 1 N m.

stem: A cyclist does 18 000 J of work against a constant resistive force while travelling 750 m. Determine the size of the resistive force.
equation: W = F s,  so F = W / s

marking.point: Rearranges to F = W / s

stem: A student pushes hard against a brick wall but the wall does not move. Explain why no work is done on the wall.

marking.point: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force
The wall does not move, so the distance is zero and the work done on it is zero

answer_text: Work done is the force multiplied by the distance moved in the direction of that force. The wall does not move at all, so the distance is zero and therefore no work is done on the wall, however hard the student pushes.

stem: A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. A force of 12 N is applied to it and the limit of proportionality is not exceeded. Calculate the extension of the spring.
equation: F = k e,  so e = F / k

marking.point: Rearranges to e = F / k

stem: Explain the difference between elastic deformation and inelastic deformation.

marking.point: In elastic deformation the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed
In inelastic deformation the object does not return to its original shape / is permanently changed

answer_text: In elastic deformation the object returns to its original shape and length once the forces are removed. In inelastic deformation it does not — the change of shape is permanent.

stem: Describe an investigation to find the relationship between the force applied to a spring and its extension.

marking.point: Hang the spring from a clamp stand and measure its original length with a ruler
Add masses of known weight one at a time and record the new length each time
Extension = new length − original length for each added weight
Plot a graph of force against extension; a straight line through the origin shows they are directly proportional

answer_text: Hang the spring vertically from a clamp stand and measure its natural length with a ruler held alongside, reading at eye level. Add 1 N weights one at a time, measuring the new length after each. Subtract the original length to get the extension for each force. Plot force on the y-axis against extension on the x-axis: a straight line through the origin shows direct proportionality, and the gradient gives the spring constant. The line curves once the limit of proportionality is passed.

stem: A force–extension graph for a spring is a straight line at first but then curves. Explain what the curved part shows.

marking.point: The straight section shows force is directly proportional to extension
The point where the line starts to curve is the limit of proportionality
Beyond it the spring extends more for each extra newton, and the deformation may become inelastic so the spring does not return to its original length

answer_text: The straight section shows that extension is directly proportional to force, so F = k e applies. Where the line begins to bend is the limit of proportionality. Beyond that point each extra newton produces a greater extension than before, and the spring may be permanently stretched — inelastic deformation — so it will not return to its original length.

stem: A force of 45 N is applied at the end of a spanner, at a perpendicular distance of 0.24 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment of the force.

marking.point: M = F d

stem: A uniform beam is balanced on a pivot. A 30 N weight sits 0.80 m to the left of the pivot. Calculate the distance to the right of the pivot at which a 48 N weight must be placed to balance the beam.
equation: For balance: F1 d1 = F2 d2,  so d2 = F1 d1 / F2

marking.point: Applies the principle of moments: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment

stem: Explain why a long-handled spanner makes it easier to undo a tight bolt than a short one.

marking.point: The moment equals force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
A longer handle gives a greater distance, so the same force produces a larger moment

answer_text: The turning effect is the moment, force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot. A longer spanner increases that distance, so the same effort force produces a bigger moment and turns the bolt more easily.

stem: A small gear drives a much larger gear. Explain the effect this has on the moment and on the speed of rotation.

marking.point: The larger gear has a greater radius, so the same force acts at a greater distance from its centre
This produces a larger moment / greater turning effect on the larger gear
The larger gear turns more slowly than the small one — the increase in moment comes at the cost of rotational speed

answer_text: Because the larger gear has a bigger radius, the force transmitted at the teeth acts at a greater distance from its centre of rotation, producing a larger moment. The trade-off is speed: the large gear completes fewer turns than the small one in the same time, so it rotates more slowly.

stem: A force of 600 N acts normally on a surface of area 0.25 m². Calculate the pressure exerted on the surface.

marking.point: p = F / A

stem: Calculate the pressure due to a column of seawater 15 m deep. The density of seawater is 1030 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg.

marking.point: p = h ρ g
151 410 Pa (accept 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa)

stem: Explain why the pressure in a liquid increases with depth.

marking.point: The pressure at a point is caused by the weight of the column of liquid above it
Deeper points have a taller column of liquid above them, so a greater weight acts on the same area
Since pressure is force per unit area, the pressure is greater at greater depth

answer_text: The pressure at a point in a liquid comes from the weight of the column of liquid directly above it. The deeper you go, the taller that column and so the greater its weight, acting on the same area. Since pressure is force per unit area, the pressure rises with depth.

stem: Explain, in terms of pressure, why an object floats in water.

marking.point: The pressure in a liquid increases with depth
So the upward pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the downward pressure on its top
This pressure difference produces a resultant upward force called upthrust
If the upthrust equals the weight of the object, the resultant force is zero and the object floats

answer_text: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, so the bottom surface of a submerged object experiences a greater pressure than its top surface. This difference produces a resultant upward force, the upthrust, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. If the upthrust equals the object's weight, the resultant force on it is zero and it floats.

stem: Explain what causes atmospheric pressure.

marking.point: Air molecules collide with a surface, exerting a force on it
Pressure is this force per unit area of the surface

answer_text: Atmospheric pressure is caused by the huge number of air molecules colliding with a surface. Each collision exerts a tiny force, and the pressure is the total force per unit area of the surface.

stem: Explain why atmospheric pressure decreases as altitude increases.

marking.point: At greater altitude there is a shorter column of air above you / less air above
So the weight of air acting on a given area is smaller
The atmosphere also becomes less dense with height, so there are fewer molecules and fewer collisions per unit area

answer_text: As you climb, there is less atmosphere left above you, so the column of air pressing down on a given area weighs less. The air also becomes less dense with height, so fewer molecules collide with each unit area every second. Both effects reduce the pressure.

stem: A sealed, partly empty plastic bottle is carried down from the top of a mountain to sea level. Explain why the bottle is crushed inwards.

marking.point: Atmospheric pressure outside the bottle is greater at sea level than on the mountain
The pressure inside is unchanged, so the outside pressure now exceeds it and the resultant inward force crushes the bottle

answer_text: At sea level the atmospheric pressure outside the bottle is much greater than it was on the mountain. The pressure of the sealed air inside has not changed, so there is now a resultant inward force on the bottle walls, which crushes it.

stem: Approximately what is atmospheric pressure at sea level?

marking.point: About 100 000 Pa

stem: A train travels 4500 m in 150 seconds at a constant speed. Calculate its speed.
equation: s = v t,  so v = s / t

marking.point: v = s / t
30 m/s

stem: Explain why an object moving in a circle at a constant speed has a continually changing velocity.

marking.point: Velocity is a vector, so it has a direction as well as a magnitude
The direction of motion changes continuously around the circle, so the velocity changes even though the speed is constant

answer_text: Velocity is a vector, so it is defined by direction as well as magnitude. Moving round a circle the direction of travel changes at every instant, so the velocity is constantly changing even though the speed stays the same.

stem: Explain the difference between distance and displacement.

marking.point: Distance is a scalar — how far an object has travelled in total, with no direction
Displacement is a vector — the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish

answer_text: Distance is a scalar: the total length of path travelled, with no direction. Displacement is a vector: the straight-line distance from the starting point to the finishing point, together with the direction.

stem: A runner covers 800 m in 200 s, then walks a further 400 m in 300 s. Calculate her average speed for the whole journey.
equation: average speed = total distance / total time

marking.point: Total distance = 800 + 400 = 1200 m
Total time = 200 + 300 = 500 s
Average speed = 1200 / 500 = 2.4 m/s

stem: State what the gradient of a distance–time graph represents, and what a horizontal line on such a graph shows.

marking.point: The gradient represents the speed of the object
A horizontal line shows the object is stationary

answer_text: The gradient of a distance–time graph gives the speed. A horizontal line has zero gradient, so it shows the object is stationary.

stem: State what the gradient of a velocity–time graph represents, and what the area under the line represents.

marking.point: The gradient represents the acceleration
The area under the line represents the distance travelled

answer_text: The gradient of a velocity–time graph gives the acceleration. The area under the line gives the distance travelled.

stem: On a velocity–time graph, an object accelerates uniformly from rest to 18 m/s in 12 s, then travels at 18 m/s for a further 20 s. Calculate the total distance travelled.
equation: distance = area under the graph = ½ × base × height + base × height

marking.point: Area of triangle = ½ × 12 × 18 = 108 m
Area of rectangle = 18 × 20 = 360 m
Total = 468 m

stem: Describe how you would find the speed of an object at a particular moment from a curved distance–time graph.

marking.point: Draw a tangent to the curve at the point of interest
Make a large right-angled triangle on the tangent and read off the change in distance and the change in time
The speed is the gradient of the tangent = change in distance ÷ change in time

answer_text: Draw a tangent that just touches the curve at the point of interest. Construct a large right-angled triangle using that tangent as the hypotenuse, and read off the change in distance and the corresponding change in time. The speed at that instant is the gradient of the tangent, change in distance divided by change in time. Using a large triangle reduces the percentage error in the readings.

stem: A car accelerates uniformly from 8.0 m/s to 26 m/s in 6.0 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

marking.point: a = change in velocity / time taken
3.0 m/s²

stem: A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest at 1.5 m/s² over a distance of 48 m. Calculate her final velocity. Use the equation v² − u² = 2 a s.

marking.point: v² = u² + 2 a s
v = 12 m/s

stem: Describe an investigation to find how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the force applied to it.

marking.point: Attach the trolley over a pulley to a hanging mass, which provides the accelerating force
Measure the acceleration using light gates and a datalogger (or a ticker tape timer)
Move masses from the trolley to the hanger to change the force while keeping the total mass constant
Repeat for several forces and plot acceleration against force; a straight line through the origin shows they are directly proportional

answer_text: Connect the trolley by a string over a pulley to a hanging mass, whose weight provides the accelerating force. Measure the acceleration with light gates and a datalogger. To change the force without changing the total mass being accelerated, transfer masses from the trolley to the hanger rather than simply adding them. Repeat for several forces and plot acceleration against force — a straight line through the origin shows acceleration is directly proportional to force. Compensating for friction by tilting the runway improves the result.

stem: A car has an acceleration of −4.0 m/s². Explain what the negative sign tells you.

marking.point: The acceleration acts in the opposite direction to the motion
so the car is slowing down / decelerating

answer_text: The negative sign means the acceleration acts in the opposite direction to the car's motion, so the car is decelerating — its velocity is decreasing by 4.0 m/s every second.

stem: State Newton's First Law of motion.

marking.point: If the resultant force on an object is zero, an object at rest stays at rest
and an object that is moving continues to move at the same speed in the same direction (constant velocity)

answer_text: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, then an object at rest stays at rest, and an object already moving continues to move at the same speed in the same straight line — at constant velocity.

stem: A resultant force of 1800 N acts on a car of mass 1200 kg. Calculate its acceleration.
equation: F = m a,  so a = F / m

marking.point: Rearranges to a = F / m
1.5 m/s²

stem: State Newton's Third Law and use it to explain how a swimmer moves forwards through water.

marking.point: When two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite
The swimmer pushes backwards on the water with her hands
The water therefore pushes forwards on the swimmer with an equal-sized force, driving her forwards

answer_text: Newton's Third Law states that whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal in size and opposite in direction. The swimmer pushes backwards on the water, so the water pushes forwards on the swimmer with an equally sized force. That forward force drives her through the pool. The two forces act on different objects, which is why they do not cancel out.

stem: Explain what is meant by inertial mass, and how it relates to the acceleration produced by a given force.

marking.point: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object
It is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration, m = F / a
For a given force, an object with greater inertial mass has a smaller acceleration

answer_text: Inertial mass measures how hard it is to change an object's velocity. It is defined as the ratio of the force applied to the acceleration produced, m = F / a. For the same applied force, an object with a larger inertial mass accelerates less.

stem: A student has a mass of 58 kg. The gravitational field strength on Earth is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the weight of the student.

marking.point: W = m g, or correct substitution 58 × 9.8
568.4 N (allow 568 N)

stem: A skydiver of mass 75 kg is falling. Her weight acts downwards and air resistance of 335 N acts upwards. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the acceleration of the skydiver.
equation: W = m g,  F = W - drag,  a = F / m

marking.point: Resultant force = 735 − 335 = 400 N
a = 400 / 75 = 5.33 m/s² (downwards)

stem: A skydiver steps out of an aircraft. Explain why she speeds up at first, and why she later falls at a constant terminal velocity.

marking.point: At first weight is greater than air resistance, so there is a resultant downward force
The resultant force causes acceleration, so she speeds up
As speed increases, air resistance increases
When air resistance equals weight the resultant force is zero, so she falls at constant (terminal) velocity

answer_text: Initially her weight is much greater than the air resistance, so there is a resultant downward force and she accelerates. Air resistance increases as she speeds up. Eventually air resistance equals her weight, the resultant force is zero, and by Newton's First Law she continues at a constant terminal velocity.

stem: The same object is taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is weaker. Which statement is correct?
choices: Its mass and weight both decrease
Its mass stays the same but its weight decreases
Its mass decreases but its weight stays the same
Its mass and weight both stay the same

marking.point: Mass stays the same but weight decreases

stem: State what is meant by stopping distance, and name its two components.

marking.point: Stopping distance is the total distance travelled from the driver seeing a hazard to the vehicle stopping
It is the sum of the thinking distance and the braking distance

answer_text: Stopping distance is the total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver spots a hazard until the vehicle comes to rest. It is the thinking distance plus the braking distance.

stem: Give three factors that increase a driver's reaction time, and explain why this is dangerous.

marking.point: Any three of: tiredness, alcohol, drugs, distractions such as a phone
A longer reaction time means the car travels further before the brakes are applied
so the thinking distance and therefore the total stopping distance increase

answer_text: Tiredness, alcohol, other drugs and distractions such as using a phone all increase reaction time. During that extra time the car continues at full speed before the brakes are even applied, which increases the thinking distance and so the total stopping distance — making a collision more likely.

stem: Explain why the braking distance of a car increases in wet or icy conditions.

marking.point: Wet or icy roads reduce the friction between the tyres and the road
So the braking force that can be applied without skidding is smaller
A smaller decelerating force means the car takes a greater distance to lose the same kinetic energy

answer_text: Water or ice reduces the friction between the tyres and the road surface, so the maximum braking force that can be applied without the car skidding is smaller. With a smaller decelerating force, the car needs a greater distance to lose the same amount of kinetic energy, so the braking distance increases.

stem: Explain why a large braking force applied at high speed can be dangerous.

marking.point: Braking transfers the kinetic energy of the car to thermal energy in the brakes
A large braking force produces a large deceleration
This can cause the brakes to overheat, or the driver to lose control / the car to skid
Because kinetic energy depends on speed squared, doubling the speed needs four times the braking distance for the same force

answer_text: Braking does work against friction, transferring the car's kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brakes. A very large braking force gives a very large deceleration, which can overheat the brakes and can make the tyres lose grip so the car skids and the driver loses control. The danger grows sharply with speed, because kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed — doubling the speed quadruples the energy that must be removed.

stem: A ball of mass 0.45 kg moves at 12 m/s. Calculate its momentum.

marking.point: p = m v
5.4 kg m/s

stem: State the principle of conservation of momentum.

marking.point: In a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it
provided no external forces act

answer_text: In a closed system the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after it, provided no external resultant force acts on the system.

stem: A trolley of mass 2.0 kg moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary trolley of mass 4.0 kg. The two trolleys stick together. Calculate their common velocity after the collision.
equation: total momentum before = total momentum after

marking.point: Momentum before = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 kg m/s
Momentum after = (2.0 + 4.0) × v
v = 1.0 m/s in the original direction

stem: A cannon recoils backwards when it fires a shell forwards. Explain this using conservation of momentum.

marking.point: Before firing the total momentum of the system is zero, since nothing is moving
Momentum is conserved, so the total momentum afterwards must also be zero
The forward momentum of the shell must be balanced by an equal backward momentum of the cannon, so the cannon recoils

answer_text: Before firing, nothing moves, so the total momentum of the cannon-and-shell system is zero. Momentum is conserved in this closed system, so the total after firing must also be zero. The shell carries forward momentum, so the cannon must carry an equal magnitude of backward momentum — it recoils. Because the cannon is far more massive, its recoil velocity is much smaller than the shell's.

stem: A ball experiences a change in momentum of 24 kg m/s in a time of 0.30 s. Calculate the average force acting on the ball.

marking.point: F = change in momentum / time taken

stem: Explain how an air bag reduces the force on a driver during a collision.

marking.point: The driver's change in momentum is the same with or without the air bag
The air bag increases the time taken for the driver to come to rest
Force equals rate of change of momentum, F = Δp / Δt
So increasing the time reduces the force on the driver, reducing injury

answer_text: The driver must lose the same amount of momentum either way — that is fixed by their mass and the speed of the car. The air bag increases the time over which that momentum change happens. Since force is the rate of change of momentum, F = Δp / Δt, a longer time means a smaller average force on the driver, so less injury.

stem: A 0.060 kg tennis ball travelling at 25 m/s is struck and rebounds straight back at 35 m/s. Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball.
equation: Δp = m v − m(−u) = m (v + u)  because the ball reverses direction

marking.point: Recognises the velocity reverses, so the velocities have opposite signs
3.6 kg m/s

stem: Explain why gymnasts land on thick, soft mats rather than on a hard floor.

marking.point: The gymnast's change in momentum on landing is the same either way
A soft mat compresses, increasing the time taken to stop
Since F = Δp / Δt, a longer stopping time gives a smaller force on the gymnast, reducing the risk of injury

answer_text: However they land, the gymnast must lose the same momentum. A thick soft mat compresses as they land, which lengthens the time over which they come to rest. Because force is the rate of change of momentum, spreading the same momentum change over a longer time reduces the average force on the body and so the risk of injury.

stem: Name two magnetic materials other than iron.

marking.point: Any two of: steel, cobalt, nickel

answer_text: Any two of: steel, cobalt, nickel.

stem: Describe the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.

marking.point: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time
An induced magnet is only magnetic while it is in a magnetic field, and loses most or all of its magnetism when removed

answer_text: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field at all times. An induced magnet only becomes magnetic when placed in a magnetic field, and loses most or all of its magnetism when taken out of that field.

stem: A steel paperclip is brought near the north pole of a magnet and is attracted. It is then brought near the south pole and is attracted again. Explain why.

marking.point: The paperclip becomes an induced magnet
The pole induced nearest the magnet is always the opposite pole, so the force is always attraction

answer_text: The paperclip becomes an induced magnet. The pole induced in the end nearest the magnet is always the opposite of the pole it is facing, so the force between them is always attraction, whichever pole is used.

stem: A student has two identical steel bars. One is a permanent magnet and one is not magnetised. Describe a test the student could do to find out which bar is the permanent magnet, using only the two bars.

marking.point: Bring one end of bar A near one end of bar B and note the force, then reverse one bar and repeat
If repulsion is observed at any point, both ends tested are like poles, so both bars are magnets
Only attraction in every combination means one bar is unmagnetised — repulsion is the only certain test for a magnet

answer_text: Bring an end of one bar close to each end of the other in turn, then reverse one bar and repeat. Attraction alone proves nothing, because an unmagnetised steel bar is attracted either way round. Repulsion can only happen between two like poles, so if repulsion is ever seen both bars are magnets; if every combination attracts, one bar is unmagnetised.

stem: Describe the magnetic field around a bar magnet, including the direction of the field lines.

marking.point: Field lines are curved loops running from one pole round to the other
The direction of a field line is from north to south (outside the magnet)
Field lines never cross, and are closest together at the poles

answer_text: The field lines form curved loops that leave the north pole, curve round the magnet and enter the south pole. By convention the direction of a field line is from north to south outside the magnet. The lines never cross, and they are closest together at the poles.

stem: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
choices: At the centre of the magnet
Halfway between the centre and a pole
The field has the same strength everywhere

marking.point: At the poles

stem: Describe how a student could use a plotting compass to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

marking.point: Place the compass near the magnet and mark a dot at each end of the needle
Move the compass so the tail of the needle is over the previous dot, and repeat to build up a line
Join the dots into a smooth curve; the compass needle points along the field, giving its direction

answer_text: Place the plotting compass close to one pole and mark dots at both ends of the needle. Move the compass so the tail of the needle sits on the last dot made, and mark the new tip. Repeat across the paper, then join the dots into a smooth curve. The needle always points along the field line, so the arrow direction gives the field direction.

stem: A plotting compass placed far from any magnet points roughly north. Explain what this tells you about the Earth.

marking.point: The Earth has its own magnetic field / behaves like a bar magnet
The field is produced by the Earth's core, which suggests the core contains a moving magnetic material such as iron

answer_text: It shows the Earth produces its own magnetic field, behaving like a giant bar magnet. The field is generated in the Earth's core, which is evidence that the core contains moving molten iron.

stem: Describe the magnetic field produced around a straight wire carrying a current.

marking.point: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to it
The field is strongest close to the wire and weakens with distance

answer_text: The field forms concentric circles around the wire, lying in planes perpendicular to it. It is strongest close to the wire and gets weaker further away. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.

stem: State three ways of increasing the strength of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid.

marking.point: Increase the current through the solenoid
Increase the number of turns per unit length of the coil
Add an iron core inside the solenoid

answer_text: Increase the current, increase the number of turns per unit length of the coil, or place an iron core inside the solenoid.

stem: Describe the shape of the magnetic field produced by a solenoid.

marking.point: Inside the solenoid the field is strong and uniform, with parallel field lines
Outside, the field is like that of a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other

answer_text: Inside the solenoid the field lines are parallel and evenly spaced, giving a strong, uniform field. Outside, the pattern is the same as that of a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.

stem: Explain why an electromagnet is more useful than a permanent magnet in a scrapyard crane.

marking.point: An electromagnet can be switched on and off by switching the current on and off
so the load can be picked up and then released where it is wanted
Its strength can also be varied by changing the current or the number of turns

answer_text: An electromagnet only produces a field while current flows, so the operator can switch it off to release the scrap exactly where it is wanted — a permanent magnet could never let go. Its strength can also be adjusted by varying the current or the number of turns.

stem: Describe how to use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.

marking.point: Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to each other
The First finger points along the magnetic Field, from north to south
The seCond finger points in the direction of the conventional Current, and the thuMb then gives the direction of the Motion or force

answer_text: Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of your left hand mutually at right angles. Point the First finger along the magnetic Field, north to south. Point the seCond finger in the direction of the conventional Current. The thuMb then points in the direction of the force, or Motion.

stem: A wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 4.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. Calculate the force on the wire.

marking.point: F = B I l

stem: Explain why a current-carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.

marking.point: The current in the wire produces its own magnetic field around it
This field interacts with the field of the permanent magnet
The two fields combine, being stronger on one side of the wire than the other, and the resulting force pushes the wire towards the weaker side

answer_text: The current produces a circular magnetic field around the wire. This interacts with the field of the magnet: on one side the two fields reinforce each other and on the other they partly cancel. The resulting imbalance pushes the wire away from the stronger region towards the weaker one, which is the motor effect.

stem: State two ways of increasing the size of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, and state when the force is zero.

marking.point: Increase the current, or increase the magnetic flux density (use a stronger magnet); a longer wire in the field also increases it
The force is zero when the wire is parallel to the magnetic field

answer_text: Increase the current, or use a stronger magnet to increase the flux density — a greater length of wire in the field also increases the force. The force is zero when the wire lies parallel to the field lines.

stem: Explain how a simple direct-current electric motor works.

marking.point: A current flows through a coil placed in a magnetic field
The two sides of the coil carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them act in opposite directions
This produces a turning effect / moment that rotates the coil
A split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction

answer_text: Current flows through a coil sitting in a magnetic field. Because the current travels in opposite directions along the two sides of the coil, the motor-effect forces on those sides act in opposite directions, creating a couple that turns the coil. Every half turn a split-ring commutator reverses the current direction in the coil, which keeps the forces turning it the same way rather than reversing.

stem: State three ways of increasing the speed of rotation of a simple electric motor.

marking.point: Increase the current through the coil
Use a stronger magnet / increase the magnetic flux density
Increase the number of turns on the coil

answer_text: Increase the current, use stronger magnets to increase the flux density, or increase the number of turns on the coil. Increasing the area of the coil also helps.

stem: Explain how a moving-coil loudspeaker converts an electrical signal into sound.

marking.point: An alternating current from the amplifier passes through a coil attached to the cone, which sits in a magnetic field
The motor effect produces a force on the coil
Because the current alternates, the force repeatedly reverses direction, so the coil and cone vibrate back and forth
The vibrating cone makes the air vibrate, producing a sound wave of the same frequency as the current

answer_text: An alternating current from the amplifier flows through a coil that is attached to the speaker cone and sits in the field of a permanent magnet. The motor effect produces a force on the coil. As the current alternates, the direction of that force reverses over and over, so the coil and the cone vibrate in and out. The moving cone pushes on the surrounding air, creating a sound wave with the same frequency as the original electrical signal.

stem: Explain what would happen to a simple d.c. motor if the split-ring commutator were replaced by fixed connections.

marking.point: The current direction in the coil would no longer reverse every half turn
so the coil would turn to the vertical position and then oscillate or stop, rather than rotating continuously

answer_text: Without the commutator the current in the coil would never reverse, so once the coil passed the vertical the forces would push it back the way it came. Instead of rotating continuously it would simply rock back and forth and come to rest.

stem: State what is meant by the generator effect.

marking.point: A potential difference is induced when an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field
or when the magnetic field through a coil changes; if the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced

answer_text: The generator effect is the inducing of a potential difference when a conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or when the magnetic field through a coil changes. If the conductor forms part of a complete circuit, a current is induced as well.

stem: State three ways of increasing the size of an induced potential difference.

marking.point: Move the conductor or magnet faster / change the field more quickly
Use a stronger magnet / increase the magnetic flux density
Increase the number of turns on the coil

answer_text: Move the magnet or conductor more quickly, use a stronger magnet, or increase the number of turns on the coil. Increasing the area of the coil also increases the induced potential difference.

stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a sensitive meter. Explain why the meter deflects, and why it returns to zero if the magnet is held still inside the coil.

marking.point: Moving the magnet changes the magnetic field through the coil, which induces a potential difference and so a current
When the magnet is held still the field through the coil is no longer changing
With no change of field there is no induced potential difference, so no current flows and the meter reads zero

answer_text: Pushing the magnet in changes the magnetic field passing through the coil. A changing field induces a potential difference, and since the circuit is complete a current flows and deflects the meter. Once the magnet is stationary the field through the coil is constant — nothing is changing — so no potential difference is induced and the meter returns to zero.

stem: Explain why an induced current always opposes the change that produced it.

marking.point: The induced current creates its own magnetic field
This field opposes the original change in field — for example repelling an approaching magnet
This must be so to conserve energy: work has to be done to move the magnet, and that work becomes the electrical energy generated

answer_text: The induced current produces its own magnetic field, and that field always acts to oppose the change that created it — repelling an approaching magnet or attracting a retreating one. It must work this way to conserve energy: if the induced field helped the motion, energy would be created from nothing. Instead work must be done against the opposing force, and that work is what becomes the electrical energy generated.

stem: Explain the difference between an alternator and a dynamo, and the type of current each produces.

marking.point: An alternator uses slip rings, so the connections to the coil never swap over
It therefore produces an alternating current, which reverses direction every half turn
A dynamo uses a split-ring commutator, which swaps the connections every half turn, so it produces a direct current that is always in the same direction

answer_text: An alternator uses slip rings, so each end of the coil stays connected to the same part of the external circuit. As the coil turns, the induced potential difference reverses every half turn, giving an alternating current. A dynamo instead uses a split-ring commutator, which swaps the connections every half turn so that the output always flows the same way — a direct current.

stem: Explain how a moving-coil microphone converts sound into an electrical signal.

marking.point: Sound waves make the diaphragm of the microphone vibrate
The diaphragm is attached to a coil, which therefore moves in a magnetic field
The generator effect induces a potential difference across the coil
The size and frequency of the induced signal depend on the amplitude and frequency of the sound wave, so the electrical signal matches the sound

answer_text: Sound waves arriving at the microphone make its diaphragm vibrate. A coil attached to the diaphragm moves with it, inside the field of a permanent magnet. Because the coil is moving relative to the field, the generator effect induces a potential difference across it. The frequency of the induced signal matches the frequency of the sound, and a louder sound moves the coil further and faster, giving a larger signal — so the electrical output faithfully copies the sound wave.

stem: Describe the shape of the output from an alternator as the coil rotates at a steady rate.

marking.point: The output is a sine wave / alternating, reversing direction every half turn
The peak output occurs when the coil is moving fastest across the field lines, and the output is zero when the coil moves parallel to them

answer_text: The output is a sine wave that reverses direction every half turn. It peaks when the coil is cutting across the field lines fastest, and falls to zero twice per revolution when the sides of the coil move parallel to the field lines.

stem: Explain what happens to the output of an alternator if the coil is rotated more quickly.

marking.point: The peak potential difference increases, because the field through the coil changes more rapidly
The frequency of the alternating output also increases, because there are more rotations per second

answer_text: Turning the coil faster makes the magnetic field through it change more rapidly, so the peak induced potential difference is larger. It also completes more rotations each second, so the frequency of the alternating output rises.

stem: Explain how a transformer works.

marking.point: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a continually changing magnetic field
The iron core carries this changing field to the secondary coil
The changing field through the secondary coil induces a potential difference across it
The ratio of the potential differences equals the ratio of the numbers of turns on the two coils

answer_text: An alternating current in the primary coil creates a magnetic field that is constantly changing in size and direction. The soft iron core channels this changing field round to the secondary coil. Because the field through the secondary is changing, a potential difference is induced across it. The ratio of the potential differences matches the ratio of turns on the two coils, which is what makes the transformer step the voltage up or down. It only works with a.c., since a steady direct current would give an unchanging field.

stem: A transformer has 120 turns on the primary coil and 3000 turns on the secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary is 240 V. Calculate the potential difference across the secondary coil.
equation: Vp / Vs = np / ns,  so Vs = Vp × ns / np

marking.point: Vs = Vp × ns / np

stem: A transformer is 100% efficient. The primary coil has a potential difference of 230 V and a current of 12 A. The secondary potential difference is 46 V. Calculate the current in the secondary coil.
equation: Vp Ip = Vs Is,  so Is = Vp Ip / Vs

marking.point: For 100% efficiency, power in = power out
Vp Ip = Vs Is

stem: Explain why the core of a transformer is made of iron.

marking.point: Iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it responds to the rapidly changing field
It concentrates and carries the magnetic field from the primary to the secondary coil, so that almost all of the field links both coils

answer_text: Iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it can follow the rapidly alternating field. It also concentrates the magnetic field and guides it from the primary coil round to the secondary, so that almost all of the field produced passes through both coils, making the transformer efficient.

stem: A block of wood has a mass of 480 g and a volume of 800 cm³. Calculate the density of the wood in g/cm³.

marking.point: ρ = m / V
0.60 g/cm³

stem: Describe how you would determine the density of a small, irregularly shaped stone.

marking.point: Measure the mass of the stone using a balance
Part-fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume
Lower the stone in fully and record the new volume; the volume of the stone is the difference
Calculate density using ρ = m / V

answer_text: Measure the mass of the stone on a balance. Part-fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the level, then lower the stone in so it is fully submerged and record the new level. The rise in level is the volume of the stone. Then use ρ = m / V. A displacement can is an alternative for larger objects.

stem: A steel bar has a density of 7800 kg/m³ and a volume of 0.0025 m³. Calculate the mass of the bar.
equation: ρ = m / V,  so m = ρ V

marking.point: Rearranges to m = ρ V

stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why a gas has a much lower density than the same substance as a liquid.

marking.point: In a gas the particles are much further apart than in a liquid
so the same number of particles (same mass) occupies a much greater volume, and density is mass per unit volume

answer_text: The particles in a gas are spread far apart, whereas in a liquid they are close together. The same mass of substance therefore occupies a far larger volume as a gas, and since density is mass divided by volume, the density is much lower.

stem: Solid carbon dioxide turns directly into a gas when it warms up. Name this change of state.

marking.point: Subliming / sublimation

stem: A sealed flask contains 0.40 kg of ice. The ice melts completely. Explain why the mass of water produced is also 0.40 kg.

marking.point: No particles enter or leave the sealed flask / number of particles is unchanged
A change of state is a physical change, so mass is conserved

answer_text: The flask is sealed so no particles are gained or lost. Melting is a physical change — only the arrangement and energy of the particles change, not their number or mass — so the mass stays at 0.40 kg.

stem: Describe the difference between the arrangement and the movement of the particles in a solid and in a gas.

marking.point: Solid: particles are close together / touching, in a regular arrangement
Solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions
Gas: particles are far apart / randomly arranged
Gas: particles move quickly in all directions / randomly

answer_text: In a solid the particles are close together in a regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. In a gas the particles are far apart and randomly arranged, and they move quickly in random directions.

stem: A physical change such as condensing is described as reversible, but burning methane is not. Explain why condensing is reversible.

marking.point: No new substance is produced / the material recovers its original properties
Only the arrangement / energy of the particles changes, so it can be changed back by heating

answer_text: Condensing produces no new substance — the particles themselves are unchanged, only their arrangement and energy. Heating the liquid reverses it and recovers the original gas with its original properties.

stem: State what is meant by the internal energy of a system.

marking.point: The total kinetic energy and potential energy
of all the particles (atoms and molecules) in the system

answer_text: Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up the system.

stem: A beaker of water is heated. Its temperature rises from 20 °C to 60 °C. Explain what happens to the internal energy of the water.

marking.point: Internal energy increases
Energy is transferred to the kinetic energy store of the particles
The particles move faster on average, which raises the temperature

answer_text: The internal energy increases. Heating transfers energy to the particles, increasing their average kinetic energy, so they move faster — and it is this rise in average kinetic energy that we measure as a rise in temperature.

stem: Ice at 0 °C is heated until it has all melted. The temperature stays at 0 °C throughout. Explain why the internal energy of the ice increases even though the temperature does not change.

marking.point: Energy is transferred to the potential energy store of the particles, not the kinetic store
The energy breaks / weakens the bonds or forces between particles
Temperature depends on average kinetic energy, which is unchanged, so the temperature stays constant

answer_text: The energy supplied goes into the potential energy of the particles rather than their kinetic energy: it weakens and breaks the forces holding the particles in the solid. Temperature depends only on the average kinetic energy, which does not change, so the temperature stays at 0 °C while internal energy rises.

stem: Which change always increases the internal energy of a fixed mass of gas?

marking.point: Heating it

stem: State what is meant by the specific latent heat of fusion of a substance.

marking.point: The energy needed to change one kilogram of the substance from solid to liquid
with no change in temperature

answer_text: The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy required to change one kilogram of a substance from solid to liquid with no change in temperature.

stem: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 334 000 J/kg. Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.25 kg of ice at 0 °C.

marking.point: E = m L

stem: A 50 W heater is used to boil water already at 100 °C. In 200 seconds it boils away 0.0044 kg of water. Determine the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water from these results.
equation: E = P t,  then L = E / m

marking.point: L = E / m
2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg (accept 2 270 000 J/kg)

stem: A graph of temperature against time for a substance being heated shows a flat section. Explain what is happening during the flat section.

marking.point: The substance is changing state (melting or boiling)
Energy is still being supplied, but it goes into breaking the forces between particles rather than increasing their kinetic energy
so the temperature stays constant while the change of state happens

answer_text: The flat section is a change of state. Energy is still being supplied, but it is used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles rather than to increase their average kinetic energy, so the temperature does not change until the change of state is complete.

stem: Explain, in terms of particles, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.

marking.point: The gas particles move rapidly in random directions
They collide with the walls of the container and exert a force on them
Pressure is the force per unit area of the wall, from the many collisions each second

answer_text: The particles of a gas move rapidly in random directions. Each time a particle collides with a wall it exerts a small force on it. The very large number of collisions every second produces a steady average force, and the pressure is this force per unit area of wall.

stem: A sealed container of gas is heated. Its volume does not change. Explain why the pressure of the gas increases.
