marking.point: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so they move faster
They hit the walls more often and with greater force
so the total force on each unit area of wall increases, increasing the pressure

answer_text: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles so they move faster. They therefore strike the walls more frequently and each collision exerts a greater force. Since the volume is fixed, the force per unit area — the pressure — rises.

stem: What does the temperature of a gas measure?
choices: The total energy of all the particles
The average kinetic energy of the particles

marking.point: The average kinetic energy of the particles

stem: Explain why the pressure of a gas in a sealed rigid container falls to almost zero when the gas is cooled towards absolute zero.

marking.point: As the temperature falls the average kinetic energy of the particles decreases, so they move more slowly
Near absolute zero the particles have almost no kinetic energy, so there are almost no collisions with the walls and the pressure is nearly zero

answer_text: Cooling reduces the average kinetic energy of the particles so they move more slowly. Approaching absolute zero they have virtually no kinetic energy, so they barely collide with the container walls and the pressure falls almost to zero.

stem: A gas at constant temperature has a volume of 0.030 m³ at a pressure of 120 000 Pa. The gas is compressed to a volume of 0.010 m³. Calculate the new pressure.
equation: p V = constant,  so p2 = p1 V1 / V2

marking.point: p1 V1 = p2 V2

stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why reducing the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature increases its pressure.

marking.point: The same number of particles is now in a smaller volume
so the particles hit the walls more frequently
The average force on each unit area of wall increases, so the pressure increases

answer_text: The same number of particles now occupies a smaller space, so each particle travels a shorter distance between collisions with the walls and hits them more often. The speeds are unchanged because the temperature is constant, but the increased rate of collisions raises the average force per unit area — the pressure.

stem: A bicycle pump is used to compress air quickly. The pump becomes warm. Explain why, in terms of work done on the gas.

marking.point: Work is done on the gas by the force pushing the piston in
This transfers energy to the internal (thermal) store of the gas
The average kinetic energy of the particles rises, so the temperature of the gas and pump increases

answer_text: Pushing the piston applies a force through a distance, so work is done on the gas. That work transfers energy to the internal energy store of the gas, raising the average kinetic energy of its particles and therefore its temperature. The warm gas then heats the pump.

stem: State the condition that must be met for the relationship pV = constant to apply to a gas.

marking.point: The temperature must stay constant
and the mass of gas must be fixed / the gas must be sealed

answer_text: The relationship holds only for a fixed mass of gas kept at constant temperature.

stem: Describe the structure of an atom, including where the mass and charge are located.

marking.point: A very small positively charged nucleus at the centre, containing protons and neutrons
Negatively charged electrons orbit the nucleus at different distances / energy levels
Almost all the mass is in the nucleus; the atom is mostly empty space

answer_text: An atom has a tiny, positively charged nucleus at its centre made of protons and neutrons, which contains almost all of the atom's mass. Negatively charged electrons orbit this nucleus at set distances corresponding to energy levels. Most of the atom is empty space.

stem: Roughly how does the radius of an atom compare with the radius of its nucleus?

marking.point: About 10 000 times larger (atom ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, nucleus ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m)

stem: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.

marking.point: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons
The positive charge of the protons exactly cancels the negative charge of the electrons

answer_text: An atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons. The positive charge on the protons is equal and opposite to the negative charge on the electrons, so the charges cancel and the atom is neutral.

stem: An atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. Explain what can happen to one of its electrons.

marking.point: The electron can move to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus
If enough energy is absorbed the electron can leave the atom altogether, ionising it

answer_text: Absorbing the radiation can lift an electron to a higher energy level further from the nucleus. If the energy absorbed is large enough the electron can escape the atom completely, leaving a positively charged ion.

stem: State what the atomic number and the mass number of an atom tell you.

marking.point: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus
Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons

answer_text: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. The mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons.

stem: An atom of an element has a mass number of 56 and an atomic number of 26. Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus.

marking.point: neutrons = mass number − atomic number

stem: Explain what is meant by two atoms being isotopes of each other.

marking.point: They have the same number of protons / same atomic number, so they are the same element
but different numbers of neutrons, so different mass numbers

answer_text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element — they have the same number of protons — but they contain different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers.

stem: Explain why two isotopes of the same element have identical chemical properties.

marking.point: Chemical behaviour is determined by the number and arrangement of electrons
Isotopes have the same number of protons and so the same number of electrons; only the neutron number differs

answer_text: Chemical reactions depend on the outer electrons, and the number of electrons is set by the number of protons. Isotopes have the same proton number, so they have identical electron arrangements — the extra neutrons affect mass but not chemistry.

stem: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.

marking.point: The atom is a ball of positive charge
with negative electrons embedded throughout it

answer_text: The plum pudding model described the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons dotted throughout it, like fruit in a pudding.

stem: In the alpha particle scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, but a very small number were deflected through large angles. Explain what these two observations showed about the structure of the atom.

marking.point: Most passing straight through shows the atom is mostly empty space
A few deflected through large angles shows there is a concentrated region of positive charge
which repels the positively charged alpha particles
Because so few were deflected, this nucleus must be very small, and it contains most of the mass

answer_text: Most alpha particles passing straight through showed that the atom is mostly empty space, which the plum pudding model could not explain. The small number deflected through large angles showed there must be a concentrated region of positive charge repelling them. Since deflections were so rare, that region — the nucleus — must be extremely small, and to turn back a fast alpha particle it must also carry most of the atom's mass.

stem: Explain why the plum pudding model was replaced by the nuclear model.

marking.point: New experimental evidence (alpha scattering) could not be explained by the plum pudding model
Scientific models are changed or replaced when new evidence does not fit them

answer_text: The alpha particle scattering results could not be explained by the plum pudding model, which predicted no large deflections. When new experimental evidence contradicts a model, scientists must modify or replace it — so the nuclear model took its place.

stem: Describe the two main changes that Niels Bohr and later James Chadwick made to the nuclear model of the atom.

marking.point: Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances / in fixed energy levels
Chadwick provided evidence for the existence of the neutron in the nucleus

answer_text: Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances in specific energy levels, which matched experimental observations. Later, Chadwick's experiments provided evidence for the neutron, a neutral particle in the nucleus.

stem: State what an alpha particle, a beta particle and a gamma ray each consist of.

marking.point: Alpha: two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus)
Beta: a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
Gamma: electromagnetic radiation / a high-energy electromagnetic wave from the nucleus

answer_text: An alpha particle is two protons and two neutrons — a helium nucleus. A beta particle is a high-speed electron ejected from the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton. A gamma ray is high-energy electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus, with no mass or charge.

stem: Compare the penetrating power and ionising power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.

marking.point: Alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating — stopped by paper or a few cm of air
Beta is moderately ionising and moderately penetrating — stopped by a few mm of aluminium
Gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating — needs thick lead or concrete to reduce it

answer_text: Alpha is the most strongly ionising but the least penetrating, stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta is less ionising but more penetrating, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma is the least ionising and the most penetrating, needing many centimetres of lead or thick concrete. Penetrating power and ionising power run in opposite directions.

stem: Which type of radiation would be most suitable for a detector that checks the thickness of aluminium sheets during manufacture?
choices: Alpha, because it is the most ionising
Beta, because it is partly absorbed by the sheet
Gamma, because it passes through unchanged
None, radiation cannot be used for this

marking.point: Beta, because the amount absorbed changes measurably with the thickness of the sheet

stem: Explain why radioactive decay is described as a random process.

marking.point: It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next, or when a particular nucleus will decay
Only the probability of decay in a given time can be stated, which is why large samples show a predictable pattern

answer_text: It is impossible to say which individual nucleus will decay next or exactly when it will happen — each nucleus has only a fixed probability of decaying in a given time. Over the huge numbers of nuclei in a real sample this randomness averages out into the predictable half-life pattern.

stem: State how the mass number and atomic number of a nucleus change when it emits an alpha particle.

marking.point: Mass number decreases by 4
Atomic number decreases by 2

answer_text: Emitting an alpha particle removes two protons and two neutrons, so the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.

stem: State how the mass number and atomic number of a nucleus change when it emits a beta particle, and explain why.

marking.point: Mass number is unchanged; atomic number increases by 1
because a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted

answer_text: The mass number stays the same and the atomic number goes up by one. This is because a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted as the beta particle, so the total number of nucleons is unchanged but there is one more proton.

stem: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) decays by alpha emission to form radon. Give the mass number and atomic number of the radon nucleus produced.

marking.point: Mass number 222
Atomic number 86

answer_text: Mass number 222 and atomic number 86, since alpha emission removes 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He.

stem: What happens to the mass number and atomic number of a nucleus when it emits only a gamma ray?
choices: Mass number decreases, atomic number stays the same

marking.point: Neither changes — gamma emission removes energy but no particles

stem: State two ways in which the half-life of a radioactive isotope can be defined.

marking.point: The time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to halve
The time taken for the count rate (or activity) from a sample to fall to half its initial value

answer_text: Half-life is the time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei in a sample to fall to half its original value. Equivalently, it is the time for the count rate or activity from the sample to halve.

stem: A radioactive source has a half-life of 6 hours. Its initial count rate is 2400 counts per minute. Calculate the count rate after 24 hours.
equation: count rate = initial ÷ 2ⁿ, where n = number of half-lives

marking.point: 24 / 6 = 4 half-lives
150 counts per minute

stem: The activity of a sample falls from 6400 Bq to 400 Bq in 12 days. Determine the half-life of the sample in days.
equation: find how many halvings, then half-life = time ÷ number of half-lives

marking.point: half-life = 12 / 4
3 days

stem: A sample contains 8.0 × 10⁸ undecayed nuclei. After 3 half-lives, calculate the net decline in the number of undecayed nuclei, expressed as a ratio of the initial number.
equation: remaining = N0 / 2ⁿ, decline ratio = (N0 − remaining) / N0

marking.point: After 3 half-lives 1/8 of the nuclei remain undecayed
So 7/8 have decayed

stem: Explain the difference between irradiation and radioactive contamination.

marking.point: Irradiation is exposing an object to radiation from an external source, without the object becoming radioactive
Contamination is having unwanted radioactive atoms on or in an object, which then keeps emitting radiation

answer_text: Irradiation means an object is exposed to radiation from a source outside it; the object does not itself become radioactive. Contamination means unwanted radioactive atoms are physically on or inside the object, so it continues to emit radiation until they are removed or decay.

stem: A scientist handling an open radioactive source wears gloves and works inside a fume cupboard. Explain how each precaution reduces risk.

marking.point: Gloves stop radioactive material getting onto the skin, preventing contamination
The fume cupboard stops radioactive dust or gas being breathed in, preventing internal contamination
Internal contamination is especially hazardous because alpha sources would then irradiate living tissue directly

answer_text: Gloves stop radioactive material transferring onto the skin, which would contaminate the scientist. The fume cupboard prevents radioactive dust or gas being inhaled, which would cause internal contamination. Internal contamination is particularly dangerous because alpha radiation, though stopped by skin from outside, is highly ionising to living tissue once inside the body.

stem: A radiographer stands behind a lead screen while taking an X-ray of a patient. What is being reduced?

marking.point: Irradiation of the radiographer

stem: Explain why the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans are published and checked by other scientists.

marking.point: Peer review allows other scientists to check the methods and conclusions for errors or bias
This makes the findings more reliable / trustworthy before they are acted on

answer_text: Publishing allows other scientists to peer review the work — checking the methods, data and conclusions for mistakes or bias, and attempting to reproduce the results. This makes the findings far more reliable before they are used to set safety limits.

stem: Describe what is meant by background radiation and give two natural sources of it.

marking.point: Background radiation is the low-level radiation that is around us all the time
Natural source: rocks such as granite, which release radon gas
Natural source: cosmic rays from space, or radioactive isotopes naturally present in food and in our bodies

answer_text: Background radiation is the low level of ionising radiation that is present around us at all times. Natural sources include radon gas released from rocks such as granite, cosmic rays reaching us from space, and naturally radioactive isotopes in food, drink and our own bodies.

stem: A medical tracer is injected into a patient so that doctors can follow it through the body. Explain why a gamma-emitting isotope with a half-life of a few hours is chosen.

marking.point: Gamma radiation is penetrating, so it passes out of the body and can be detected outside
Gamma is weakly ionising, so it does less damage to the patient's tissue than alpha or beta would
A half-life of a few hours is long enough to complete the scan but short enough that the activity soon falls away

answer_text: Gamma radiation penetrates body tissue, so it can escape and be detected by a camera outside the patient. It is also only weakly ionising, so it does relatively little damage to healthy cells. A half-life of a few hours is long enough for the scan to be completed but short enough that the tracer's activity falls to a safe level soon afterwards.

stem: Explain why a radioactive source used to sterilise surgical instruments should have a long half-life.

marking.point: Its activity stays roughly constant over a long period
so it does not need replacing often and gives a consistent dose

answer_text: A long half-life means the activity decreases only slowly, so the source gives a consistent dose over a long period and does not have to be replaced frequently.

stem: Explain why background radiation must be measured and subtracted when finding the count rate from a radioactive source.

marking.point: The detector also registers counts from background radiation, not just from the source
Subtracting the background count gives the true count rate due to the source alone

answer_text: A detector registers background radiation as well as radiation from the source, so the raw reading is too high. Measuring the background count with the source removed and subtracting it gives the corrected count rate due to the source alone.

stem: Describe what happens during nuclear fission of a uranium-235 nucleus.

marking.point: The nucleus absorbs a neutron and becomes unstable
It splits into two smaller nuclei of roughly similar size
Two or three neutrons are released along with energy (as gamma radiation and kinetic energy of the products)

answer_text: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, which makes it unstable. It then splits into two smaller daughter nuclei of roughly similar size, releasing two or three further neutrons plus energy — carried away as gamma radiation and as kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons.

stem: Explain how a chain reaction occurs in a nuclear reactor, and how control rods are used to keep it steady.

marking.point: Each fission releases two or three neutrons, which can be absorbed by other nuclei and cause further fissions
If uncontrolled, the number of fissions increases rapidly and the reaction runs away
Control rods absorb some of the neutrons, so on average one neutron per fission causes the next fission, keeping the rate steady

answer_text: Each fission releases two or three neutrons, and each of those can be absorbed by another uranium nucleus and trigger a further fission — so the number of fissions can grow rapidly. Control rods, made of a neutron-absorbing material such as boron, are lowered into the core to soak up surplus neutrons, so that on average exactly one neutron from each fission goes on to cause the next. This holds the reaction rate steady.

stem: Describe what happens during nuclear fusion.

marking.point: Two light nuclei join together to form a single heavier nucleus
Some of the mass is converted into energy, which is released as radiation

answer_text: In nuclear fusion two light nuclei join to form a single heavier nucleus. Some of the mass of the original nuclei is converted into energy, which is released as radiation.

stem: Explain why nuclear fusion is very difficult to achieve on Earth, even though it happens continuously in the Sun.

marking.point: Both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other strongly (electrostatic repulsion)
Extremely high temperatures and pressures are needed to give the nuclei enough kinetic energy to overcome this repulsion
The Sun provides these conditions through its enormous gravitational force, which is hard to reproduce or contain on Earth

answer_text: Both nuclei carry positive charge, so there is a strong electrostatic repulsion pushing them apart. Overcoming it requires enormous temperatures and pressures so the nuclei move fast enough to get close enough to fuse. In the Sun these conditions are produced by its immense gravitational compression; on Earth they are extremely hard to create and to contain.

stem: Describe what our solar system contains.

marking.point: The Sun, which is a star at the centre
The eight planets, which orbit the Sun, and dwarf planets such as Pluto
Natural satellites (moons) which orbit the planets, plus asteroids and comets

answer_text: At the centre is the Sun, a star. Eight planets orbit it, along with dwarf planets such as Pluto. Natural satellites — moons — orbit the planets, and the system also contains asteroids and comets.

stem: Describe how our Sun was formed.

marking.point: A cloud of dust and gas, called a nebula, was pulled together by gravity
As the material contracted the temperature and pressure at the centre rose enormously
When it was hot enough, hydrogen nuclei began to fuse and the star began to shine

answer_text: A vast cloud of dust and gas — a nebula — was pulled together by gravitational attraction. As the material fell inwards the temperature and pressure at the centre rose enormously. Eventually conditions were extreme enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium, releasing energy, and the Sun began to shine as a main sequence star.

stem: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our solar system?

marking.point: The Milky Way

stem: Explain why the Sun is in a stable state during its main sequence period.

marking.point: The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from the energy released by fusion
These two effects are equal and opposite, so the star neither collapses nor expands

answer_text: Gravity pulls the material of the star inwards, while the enormous outward pressure produced by fusion in the core pushes outwards. During the main sequence these two are balanced, so the star stays the same size — it neither collapses nor expands.

stem: Describe the life cycle of a star about the same size as the Sun, from nebula to its final stage.

marking.point: A nebula of dust and gas is pulled together by gravity to form a protostar
Fusion begins and the star becomes a stable main sequence star
When the hydrogen runs low it expands to become a red giant
It then throws off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf which cools and fades to a black dwarf

answer_text: Gravity pulls a nebula of dust and gas together into a protostar, which heats up until fusion begins and it becomes a stable main sequence star. When the hydrogen in the core runs low, it swells into a red giant. It then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving behind a hot dense core — a white dwarf — which gradually cools and fades to a black dwarf.

stem: Describe how the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun differs after the main sequence stage.

marking.point: It expands into a red super giant rather than a red giant
It then explodes as a supernova
The remaining core forms a neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough

answer_text: A much more massive star swells into a red super giant instead of a red giant. It then explodes as a supernova, scattering its outer layers into space. What remains of the core collapses into a neutron star, or, if the original star was massive enough, into a black hole.

stem: Explain how elements heavier than iron came to exist in the universe.

marking.point: Fusion in stars can only produce elements up to iron
Elements heavier than iron are produced in the explosion of a supernova
The supernova distributes these elements through space, where they can form new planets

answer_text: Nuclear fusion inside a star can build up elements only as far as iron. Elements heavier than iron are created in the immense energies of a supernova explosion. That explosion also scatters the material out across space, where it can later be incorporated into new stars and planets — which is why such elements are found on Earth.

stem: Explain why a star expands to become a red giant when the hydrogen in its core runs low.

marking.point: With less fusion in the core, the outward pressure falls and the core contracts, which raises the temperature
Fusion of heavier elements and of hydrogen in the outer shell then pushes the outer layers outwards, so the star expands and cools at the surface

answer_text: As the core hydrogen is used up, fusion in the core slows and the outward pressure drops, so the core contracts and becomes hotter. This drives fusion of heavier elements and of hydrogen in a shell outside the core, and the extra energy pushes the outer layers far outwards. The expanded surface is cooler, so it glows red.

stem: Explain why an object moving in a circular orbit at a constant speed is accelerating.

marking.point: Acceleration means a change in velocity, and velocity is a vector
The direction of motion changes continuously around the orbit, so the velocity changes even at constant speed
The gravitational force acts towards the centre, providing the centripetal force that produces this change

answer_text: Acceleration is a change of velocity, and velocity includes direction. In a circular orbit the direction of motion changes continuously, so the velocity is always changing even though the speed is constant. Gravity provides the force towards the centre of the orbit that causes this change — the centripetal force.

stem: Explain what happens to the speed of a satellite in a stable orbit if it moves into a lower orbit, closer to the Earth.

marking.point: Closer to the Earth the gravitational force on the satellite is greater
For a stable orbit the gravitational force must exactly provide the centripetal force needed
A greater force requires a greater speed at that smaller radius, so the satellite must travel faster

answer_text: Closer to the Earth the gravitational force acting on the satellite is stronger. For the orbit to remain stable, that force must exactly supply the centripetal force required for circular motion at that radius. A stronger force at a smaller radius corresponds to a higher orbital speed, so satellites in lower orbits travel faster and complete an orbit in less time.

stem: State what provides the force that keeps a planet in orbit around the Sun, and state the direction in which this force acts.

marking.point: The gravitational force of attraction between the Sun and the planet
It acts towards the centre of the orbit, that is towards the Sun

answer_text: The gravitational attraction between the Sun and the planet provides the force. It acts towards the centre of the orbit — towards the Sun.

stem: Explain the difference between a natural satellite and an artificial satellite, giving one example of each.

marking.point: A natural satellite is a naturally occurring object in orbit, such as the Moon orbiting the Earth
An artificial satellite is one built and launched by humans, such as a communications or weather satellite

answer_text: A natural satellite is a naturally occurring body in orbit around a planet, such as the Moon orbiting the Earth. An artificial satellite is one built and put into orbit by humans, such as a communications or weather satellite.

stem: Explain what is meant by red-shift.

marking.point: Light from a receding galaxy is observed to have a longer wavelength / lower frequency than expected
The observed wavelength is shifted towards the red end of the visible spectrum

answer_text: Red-shift is the observation that light from a galaxy moving away from us arrives with a longer wavelength and lower frequency than it was emitted with, so its features are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.

stem: Explain how observations of red-shift provide evidence that the universe is expanding.

marking.point: Light from distant galaxies shows red-shift, so those galaxies are moving away from us
The more distant a galaxy, the greater its red-shift
So more distant galaxies are moving away faster
This is observed in all directions, which is what would be seen if space itself were expanding everywhere

answer_text: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, showing they are moving away from us. Crucially, the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift, so the faster it is receding. This pattern holds in every direction we look, which is exactly what would be observed if space itself were expanding everywhere rather than our galaxy being at some special centre.

stem: Explain why observations of supernovae in distant galaxies have changed scientists' views about the expansion of the universe.

marking.point: Observations since 1998 suggest distant galaxies are moving away ever faster
So the expansion of the universe appears to be accelerating, not slowing down as expected
This is attributed to dark energy, and it shows scientific models change when new evidence appears

answer_text: Since 1998, measurements using supernovae in very distant galaxies have shown that those galaxies are receding ever faster. This means the expansion of the universe is accelerating, rather than slowing under gravity as had been expected. The cause is attributed to dark energy, which is still poorly understood — a good example of how scientific models are revised when new evidence emerges.

stem: State what the Big Bang theory says about the beginning of the universe.

marking.point: The universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense
It has been expanding ever since, and cooling as it expands

answer_text: The Big Bang theory states that the universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region, and that it has been expanding and cooling ever since.

stem: Explain the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.

marking.point: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer

answer_text: In a transverse wave the particles or fields oscillate at right angles to the direction in which the wave transfers energy. In a longitudinal wave they oscillate parallel to that direction, producing compressions and rarefactions.

stem: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?

marking.point: A sound wave in air

stem: A duck floats on a pond as water waves pass beneath it. The duck bobs up and down but does not move towards the shore. Explain what this shows about waves.

marking.point: Waves transfer energy from place to place
They do not transfer matter / the water itself does not travel with the wave
The water and the duck oscillate about a fixed position as the wave passes through

answer_text: It shows that waves transfer energy, not matter. The water particles — and the duck floating on them — simply oscillate up and down about a fixed point as the wave passes through. The energy travels towards the shore, but the water does not.

stem: Define the amplitude and the wavelength of a wave.

marking.point: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) position
Wavelength is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave

answer_text: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed position. Wavelength is the distance from any point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, for example crest to crest.

stem: A wave has a frequency of 400 Hz and a wavelength of 0.85 m. Calculate its speed.

marking.point: v = f λ

stem: A wave has a period of 0.025 s. Calculate its frequency.

marking.point: f = 1 / T
40 Hz

stem: Define the frequency and the period of a wave, and state the unit of each.

marking.point: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz)
Period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, measured in seconds (s)

answer_text: Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz. Period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, measured in seconds. They are reciprocals of each other.

stem: A radio wave travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and has a wavelength of 250 m. Calculate its frequency.
equation: v = f λ,  so f = v / λ

marking.point: Rearranges to f = v / λ

stem: Describe a method for measuring the speed of water waves in a ripple tank.

marking.point: Use a motorised dipper to produce waves of constant frequency, and read the frequency from the signal generator
Use a strobe or a still image to freeze the pattern, and measure the length of several wavelengths with a ruler
Divide by the number of waves to find one wavelength
Calculate the speed using v = f λ

answer_text: Set up a ripple tank with a motorised dipper driven by a signal generator, and read the frequency directly from the generator. Freeze the wave pattern using a strobe light or by photographing the projected shadow, then measure the length of ten wavelengths with a ruler and divide by ten to find one wavelength — measuring several reduces the percentage error. Then calculate the speed from v = f λ.

stem: Describe how you could measure the speed of a wave travelling along a stretched string.

marking.point: Use a vibration generator driven by a signal generator to set up a standing wave on the string, and read the frequency from the generator
Measure the length of a whole number of half-wavelengths (loops) with a metre rule, and work out one wavelength
Calculate the speed using v = f λ

answer_text: Attach the string to a vibration generator driven by a signal generator, with a mass over a pulley providing tension. Adjust the frequency until a clear standing wave forms, and read the frequency from the generator. Measure the length of several loops with a metre rule — each loop is half a wavelength — to find the wavelength. Then use v = f λ.

stem: In a ripple tank, 12 complete waves pass a point in 4.0 seconds. The distance across 5 wavelengths is measured as 0.60 m. Calculate the speed of the waves.
equation: f = n / t,  λ = d / k,  v = f λ

stem: Explain why measuring the length of ten wavelengths and dividing by ten gives a more accurate value than measuring one wavelength.

marking.point: The absolute uncertainty in the ruler reading is the same either way
Measuring a larger distance makes that uncertainty a smaller percentage of the measurement, reducing the percentage error

answer_text: The uncertainty in reading the ruler is roughly the same however long the distance measured. Measuring ten wavelengths makes that fixed uncertainty a much smaller fraction of the total reading, so the percentage error in the calculated wavelength is much smaller.

stem: State the law of reflection, and explain what is meant by the normal.

marking.point: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The normal is the construction line drawn at right angles to the surface at the point where the ray strikes it, and all angles are measured from it

answer_text: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. The normal is a construction line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray hits it; both angles are measured from this line, not from the surface.

stem: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block and changes direction. Explain why refraction occurs.

marking.point: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air
If the ray meets the boundary at an angle, one side of the wavefront slows before the other
This makes the ray change direction, bending towards the normal as it enters the denser medium

answer_text: Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. When the ray meets the boundary at an angle, one edge of the wavefront enters the glass and slows down before the other edge does. That difference swings the wavefront round, so the ray changes direction — bending towards the normal on entering the denser medium.

stem: Describe an investigation to find how the angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence for light entering a glass block.

marking.point: Place the glass block on paper, draw round it, and mark the normal at the point of entry
Shine a ray from a ray box at a measured angle of incidence to the normal
Mark the incident and emergent rays with crosses, remove the block and join them to trace the refracted ray
Measure the angle of refraction with a protractor and repeat for several angles of incidence

answer_text: Place the glass block on plain paper, draw round its outline and construct a normal at the point where the ray will enter. Direct a single ray from a ray box at a measured angle of incidence, and mark the incoming ray and the ray leaving the block with crosses. Remove the block and join the crosses to reveal the path inside, then measure the angle of refraction from the normal with a protractor. Repeat for a range of angles of incidence and tabulate the results.

stem: A ray of light enters a glass block exactly along the normal. Explain why it does not change direction.

marking.point: The whole wavefront reaches the boundary at the same moment
so both sides slow down together and there is no bending, although the speed still decreases

answer_text: Travelling along the normal, the entire wavefront meets the boundary at the same instant, so every part of it slows down simultaneously. With no difference in timing across the wavefront there is nothing to swing it round, so the ray continues straight — though it does still slow down.

stem: Describe how a sound wave travels through a steel rail.

marking.point: Sound is a longitudinal wave
The particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer
This produces compressions and rarefactions that pass along the rail

answer_text: Sound travels as a longitudinal wave. The particles of the steel vibrate backwards and forwards parallel to the direction the wave travels, producing compressions and rarefactions that pass energy along the rail.

stem: A sound wave of frequency 250 Hz travels through steel at 5000 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the sound wave in the steel.
equation: v = f λ,  so λ = v / f

marking.point: λ = v / f

stem: A sound wave passes from air into water. Its frequency does not change, but its wavelength does. Explain why.

marking.point: The frequency is set by the source, so it is unchanged
Sound travels faster in water than in air
Since v = f λ and f is constant, a greater speed means a longer wavelength

answer_text: Frequency is fixed by the source, so it does not change on entering the water. Sound travels faster in water than in air, and because v = f λ with f constant, the increase in speed must produce a longer wavelength.

stem: The normal human hearing range is 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Explain why this range is limited.

marking.point: Hearing depends on the ear drum and other parts vibrating with the sound wave
These only vibrate efficiently over a limited range of frequencies

answer_text: Hearing works by the sound wave making the ear drum and the bones behind it vibrate. Those parts only vibrate efficiently over a limited band of frequencies, which sets the 20 Hz to 20 kHz range.

stem: State what is meant by ultrasound, and give one medical use of it.

marking.point: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz, above the range of human hearing
Used for pre-natal scanning of a foetus (or to detect internal damage / break up kidney stones)

answer_text: Ultrasound is sound of frequency greater than 20 000 Hz, above the upper limit of human hearing. It is used medically for pre-natal scanning of a foetus, because it is non-ionising and so safer than X-rays.

stem: An ultrasound pulse is sent into the sea and reflects from the seabed. It returns after 0.12 s. The speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the seabed.
equation: s = v t, then halve because the pulse travels there and back

marking.point: Total distance = v × t = 1500 × 0.12 = 180 m
Recognises this is the distance there and back
Depth = 180 / 2

stem: Explain how ultrasound is used to produce an image of a foetus.

marking.point: Ultrasound pulses are directed into the body from a transducer
At each boundary between different tissues, part of the wave is reflected back
The time taken for each reflection to return is used to calculate the depth of that boundary, and a computer builds these into an image

answer_text: A transducer sends pulses of ultrasound into the body. Whenever a pulse meets a boundary between two different media — for example tissue and fluid — part of it is reflected back. The transducer detects these echoes, and since the speed in tissue is known, the time delay of each echo gives the depth of that boundary. A computer assembles all these depths into an image.

stem: Explain how the study of seismic waves has provided evidence about the structure of the Earth.

marking.point: P-waves are longitudinal and travel through both solids and liquids, while S-waves are transverse and travel only through solids
S-waves are not detected on the far side of the Earth, creating a shadow zone
This shows part of the core must be liquid; the paths of the waves also curve due to changing density, showing the Earth is layered

answer_text: P-waves are longitudinal and pass through both solids and liquids, whereas S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids. Earthquake monitoring shows an S-wave shadow zone on the far side of the Earth, which is evidence that part of the core is liquid. The way wave paths curve and refract as they travel also shows that the Earth's density changes with depth, confirming a layered structure.

stem: List the seven groups of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength.

marking.point: Gamma, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared
microwaves, radio waves

answer_text: In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves.

stem: State three properties that all electromagnetic waves have in common.

marking.point: They are all transverse waves
They all travel at the same speed through a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s)
They all transfer energy from a source to an absorber

answer_text: All electromagnetic waves are transverse, all travel at the same speed of 3 × 10⁸ m/s through a vacuum, and all transfer energy from a source to an absorber.

stem: Which group of the electromagnetic spectrum has the highest frequency?

marking.point: Gamma rays

stem: Explain why the electromagnetic spectrum is described as continuous, even though it is usually drawn as seven separate groups.

marking.point: The wavelength and frequency vary smoothly, with no gaps between the groups
The boundaries between the groups are chosen for convenience rather than marking any sudden physical change

answer_text: Wavelength and frequency vary smoothly across the whole spectrum with no gaps. The division into seven named groups is made for convenience, based on how the waves are produced and used — there is no abrupt physical change at the boundaries.

stem: Explain how radio waves are produced.

marking.point: Oscillations in an electrical circuit cause electrons to oscillate in an aerial
The oscillating charges emit radio waves with the same frequency as the oscillation

answer_text: An alternating current in a circuit makes electrons oscillate back and forth in an aerial. These oscillating charges radiate radio waves whose frequency matches the frequency of the oscillation.

stem: Explain how changes in the atoms and nuclei of a substance can produce electromagnetic waves, and how electromagnetic waves can cause changes in atoms.

marking.point: When an electron drops to a lower energy level it emits electromagnetic radiation
Changes in the nucleus of an atom can produce gamma rays
Absorbing electromagnetic radiation can raise an electron to a higher energy level, or remove it entirely, ionising the atom

answer_text: When an electron in an atom falls from a higher to a lower energy level, the energy difference is emitted as electromagnetic radiation — this is how visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays can arise. Changes within the nucleus itself produce gamma rays. The process also runs the other way: absorbing electromagnetic radiation can lift an electron to a higher energy level, or if the energy is great enough, knock it out of the atom altogether and ionise it.

stem: Explain what happens to a wave when it is refracted at the boundary between two materials.

marking.point: Its speed changes, and its wavelength changes with it
Its frequency stays the same, and its direction changes unless it meets the boundary along the normal

answer_text: The wave changes speed, and because the frequency is fixed by the source, the wavelength changes too. Unless it crosses the boundary along the normal, the wave also changes direction.

stem: Explain why different substances absorb, transmit, reflect or refract electromagnetic waves in ways that depend on the wavelength.

marking.point: How a wave interacts depends on how its energy compares with the structure and energy levels of the material
Since energy depends on wavelength, the same material behaves differently towards different parts of the spectrum

answer_text: The way a wave interacts with a material depends on how the wave's energy compares with the spacing of the material's atoms and its electron energy levels. Because the energy of an electromagnetic wave depends on its wavelength, one material can transmit some wavelengths while absorbing or reflecting others — glass transmits visible light but absorbs much ultraviolet, for example.

stem: Give one use of microwaves, one use of infrared and one use of X-rays.

marking.point: Microwaves: satellite communications or cooking food
Infrared: electrical heaters, cooking, or infrared cameras / remote controls
X-rays: medical imaging of bones, or security scanning

answer_text: Microwaves are used for satellite communications and for cooking food. Infrared is used in electrical heaters, grills and infrared cameras, and in TV remote controls. X-rays are used for medical imaging of bones and for security scanning.

stem: Explain why ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are hazardous to people, and state which is most hazardous.

marking.point: They are ionising, so they can remove electrons from atoms in living cells
This can damage cells or cause mutations in DNA, which may lead to cancer
Gamma rays are the most hazardous because they carry the most energy and penetrate deepest into the body

answer_text: These three are ionising radiations: they carry enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms in living tissue. That can kill cells or cause mutations in DNA which may lead to cancer — ultraviolet causes skin cancer and eye damage, for instance. Gamma rays are the most hazardous because they have the highest energy and penetrate furthest into the body.

stem: Explain why radio waves rather than visible light are used to broadcast television signals over long distances.

marking.point: Radio waves have long wavelengths, so they can diffract around obstacles and be reflected by the atmosphere
They are not absorbed or blocked by buildings and weather as readily as visible light, so they travel much further

answer_text: Radio waves have very long wavelengths, so they diffract around hills and buildings and can be reflected by the upper atmosphere. Visible light is blocked by almost any obstacle and scattered by the atmosphere, so it would not reach receivers over long distances.

stem: Explain why radiographers who take many X-ray images each day must take precautions, while a patient having a single X-ray does not.

marking.point: X-rays are ionising and the risk depends on the total dose received
A patient receives a single small dose, where the benefit of diagnosis outweighs the small risk
A radiographer would accumulate a large dose over many patients, so they stand behind a lead screen or leave the room, and wear a dose badge

answer_text: X-rays are ionising, and the risk of cell damage builds with the total dose received. A patient has one short exposure, and the diagnostic benefit clearly outweighs that small risk. A radiographer, though, would accumulate the dose from every patient all day, so they stand behind a lead screen or leave the room, and wear a badge that monitors their cumulative exposure.

stem: Explain the difference between how a convex lens and a concave lens affect parallel rays of light.

marking.point: A convex (converging) lens brings parallel rays together at the principal focus
A concave (diverging) lens spreads parallel rays out, so they appear to come from a principal focus behind the lens

answer_text: A convex, or converging, lens refracts parallel rays so that they meet at the principal focus. A concave, or diverging, lens spreads parallel rays apart so that they appear to come from a principal focus on the same side as the incoming light.

stem: An object of height 12 mm produces an image of height 42 mm in a convex lens. Calculate the magnification.

marking.point: magnification = image height / object height
3.5 (magnification has no unit)

stem: Explain the difference between a real image and a virtual image.

marking.point: A real image is formed where light rays actually meet, so it can be projected onto a screen
A virtual image is formed where rays only appear to come from, so it cannot be projected onto a screen
A concave lens always produces a virtual image; a convex lens produces a virtual image when the object is closer than the focal length

answer_text: A real image forms where light rays genuinely converge, so it can be captured on a screen placed at that point. A virtual image forms where rays only appear to originate when traced backwards, so no light actually arrives there and it cannot be projected. Concave lenses always give virtual images; a convex lens gives one only when the object is nearer than the focal length, as in a magnifying glass.

stem: State what is meant by the principal focus and the focal length of a convex lens.

marking.point: The principal focus is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis are brought together
The focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus

answer_text: The principal focus is the point at which rays travelling parallel to the principal axis converge after passing through the lens. The focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to that principal focus.

stem: Which of these gives the approximate wavelength range of visible light?

marking.point: 400 nm to 700 nm

stem: A jumper looks red in white light. Explain why.

marking.point: White light contains all the colours of the visible spectrum
The surface reflects (or scatters) red light
It absorbs the other wavelengths, so only red reaches the eye

answer_text: White light contains all the visible wavelengths. The surface of the jumper reflects the red wavelengths and absorbs the rest, so only red light reaches the eye and the jumper appears red.

stem: The same red jumper is viewed in a room lit only by blue light. Explain what colour it appears.

marking.point: It appears black / very dark
There is no red light to reflect, and the blue light is absorbed, so almost no light reaches the eye

answer_text: It appears black. There is no red light present for it to reflect, and it absorbs the blue light falling on it, so almost no light is reflected to the eye.

stem: Describe the difference between specular reflection and diffuse reflection.

marking.point: Specular reflection happens at a smooth surface and diffuse reflection at a rough surface
In specular reflection parallel rays are reflected in a single direction, giving a clear image
In diffuse reflection the rays are scattered in many directions, so no image is formed

answer_text: Specular reflection occurs at a smooth surface such as a mirror: parallel rays are all reflected in the same direction, so a clear image is formed. Diffuse reflection occurs at a rough surface: the normal is different at each point, so rays scatter in many directions and no image is formed.

stem: Describe an investigation to find how the amount of infrared radiation emitted by a surface depends on the nature of that surface.

marking.point: Fill a Leslie cube with hot water; its four faces have different surfaces such as matt black, shiny black, matt white and shiny silver
Hold an infrared detector a fixed distance from each face in turn
Record the detector reading for each surface
Keep the water temperature and the distance the same for each face; the matt black surface gives the highest reading

answer_text: Fill a Leslie cube — whose four vertical faces are matt black, shiny black, matt white and shiny silver — with hot water. Hold an infrared detector a fixed distance from one face and record the reading, then repeat for each of the other faces at exactly the same distance. Keep the water temperature constant by working quickly. The matt black face gives the largest reading, showing it is the best emitter of infrared, and the shiny silver face the smallest.

stem: State what is meant by a perfect black body.

marking.point: An object that absorbs all of the radiation that falls on it, reflecting and transmitting none
It is also the best possible emitter of radiation

answer_text: A perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it — none is reflected or transmitted. It is also the best possible emitter of radiation.

stem: Explain how the temperature of the Earth is affected by the balance between the radiation it absorbs and the radiation it emits.

marking.point: The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun and emits radiation into space
If the rate of absorption equals the rate of emission, the temperature stays constant
If absorption exceeds emission the Earth's temperature rises
Greenhouse gases absorb some of the emitted infrared and re-radiate it back, reducing the rate of energy loss and raising the temperature

answer_text: The Earth continually absorbs radiation from the Sun and emits infrared radiation into space. When those two rates are equal the average temperature stays constant. If absorption exceeds emission the temperature rises, and if emission exceeds absorption it falls. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb part of the outgoing infrared and re-radiate some back to the surface, which lowers the net rate of energy loss and so raises the equilibrium temperature.

stem: Explain what happens to the intensity and the wavelength distribution of the radiation emitted by an object as its temperature increases.

marking.point: The intensity of the emitted radiation increases at every wavelength
The peak of the distribution shifts to shorter wavelengths

answer_text: As the temperature rises, the object emits more radiation at every wavelength, so the total intensity increases. The peak of the distribution also moves to shorter wavelengths — which is why a heated metal glows first red and then white.
